source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of exact tab-separated Greek payload, retaining whitespace and variant markers.

notes: Paul opposes leader-centered factions by asking whether Christ has been divided and whether Paul was crucified or became their baptismal name.
‘Foolishness,’ ‘weakness,’ wisdom, and power remain in deliberate paradox around the crucified Messiah.
The calling language names social status and power. It does not romanticize deprivation; it denies human boasting before God.
vocabulary: Redemption or release secured at a cost.

notes: The pinned Greek reads ‘testimony of God’; some witnesses read ‘mystery of God.’
‘Mature’ can also mean complete; the word does not identify a secret spiritual elite.
The final phrase can mean interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people, combining spiritual things with spiritual words, or explaining spiritual realities spiritually.
‘Natural’ and ‘spiritual’ describe relation to God's Spirit in this argument, not a license for unaccountable superiority.
vocabulary: A divine purpose once hidden and now disclosed.
Natural, merely human, or lacking the Spirit.

notes: Paul calls factional jealousy evidence of immaturity, not proof that embodied life itself is evil.
The Greek can call Paul and Apollos ‘God's coworkers’ while the field and building belong to God; it does not make the Corinthians coworkers in this sentence.
The builder may be saved ‘as through fire’ while the work is lost; the image is retained without constructing a later doctrine from it.
The pronouns are plural: the community together is God's temple, and destroying it brings a severe warning.
vocabulary: Made of flesh; fleshly or immature in context.

notes: Paul rejects premature human verdicts without claiming his own conscience proves innocence; the Lord exposes hidden motives.
The ‘reigning’ language is irony. The apostles' hunger, exposure, beatings, displacement, and public humiliation are translated as real harm.
Paul's father language describes his role through the gospel; it is not biological paternity or unlimited authority.
The rod is a real disciplinary image, contrasted with love and gentleness.
vocabulary: Steward or household manager entrusted with another's goods.

notes: ‘His father's wife’ normally identifies a stepmother; the text does not call her the man's biological mother.
Handing the man to Satan ‘for destruction of the flesh’ is severe and disputed. The stated purpose is that his spirit may be saved.
Paul explicitly limits this communal separation to a person claiming insider status; God judges outsiders.
The Passover and unleavened-bread images shape the community's response to tolerated harm.

The two Greek sexual terms are distinct and heavily debated in modern application. The main text represents their male sexual roles without expanding them into a claim about every form of orientation or relationship.
The repeated ‘everything is permissible’ and food/stomach lines likely quote Corinthian slogans, which Paul immediately qualifies.
Paul grounds sexual ethics in bodily union, resurrection, the Spirit's indwelling, and belonging to God; the body is not treated as disposable.
Paul names accepting wrong as preferable to believers using public litigation to wrong and defraud one another; he does not call abuse harmless.
vocabulary: Literally soft; here a disputed term for a passive male sexual role.
A rare term literally combining male and bed, referring to male-male sex in this list.

notes: ‘Not to touch a woman’ is a sexual euphemism and likely repeats a claim from the Corinthians' letter before Paul qualifies it.
Marital bodily authority and sexual obligation are stated symmetrically; temporary abstinence requires mutual agreement and is time-limited.
When an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer is ‘not enslaved’; the passage's call to peace should not be used to require coercive control.
The Greek can mean ‘make use of your present condition’ or ‘take the opportunity for freedom.’ The main text chooses freedom while preserving the slavery setting.

Paul repeatedly marks this as situational counsel during a ‘present crisis,’ not a declaration that marriage is sinful. Verses 36–38 are grammatically disputed and may concern a fiancé or a father/guardian.
vocabulary: Enslave or bind as a slave.
Undistracted or without being pulled away.

notes: ‘We all have knowledge’ is likely a Corinthian slogan. Paul immediately contrasts knowledge that inflates with love that builds.
A conscience formed by former idol worship can be wounded; the knowledgeable person's freedom is judged by its effect on a person for whom Christ died.
Paul acknowledges many beings called gods and lords while confessing one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
vocabulary: Food offered in sacrifice to an idol.
Build up or strengthen a community.

notes: The phrase describes a believing wife traveling with an apostle; it does not refer merely to a female assistant.
Paul applies the unmuzzled-ox command to material support for workers while stating that he personally did not use this right in Corinth.
The Greek sentence breaks off after Paul's preference to die; the interruption and force are retained.
Paul's self-enslavement is a voluntary mission metaphor from a free person; it does not make ancient enslavement benign.
The verb can describe striking below the eye or treating the body severely. The translation retains the harsh bodily image rather than spiritualizing it.
vocabulary: Seal, mark of validation, or ownership.

notes: The pinned text reads twenty-three thousand, distinct from the twenty-four thousand in Numbers 25's broader account.
The pinned Greek reads ‘test Christ’; some witnesses read ‘test the Lord.’
The same word can mean temptation or trial. The promised ‘way out’ enables endurance; it does not deny severe circumstances.
Participation at the Lord's table is contrasted with participation in sacrificial meals offered to demons; the argument is about embodied communal allegiance.
‘Everything is permissible’ is likely a Corinthian slogan. Paul answers with benefit and communal upbuilding.
‘Head’ can carry senses of authority, prominence, or source. The main text retains the metaphor and gendered sequence.
The precise head covering and the appeal to nature are culturally and grammatically disputed. Women are explicitly praying and prophesying; verse 10 says a woman has authority over her head.
The meal's abuse includes hunger among those who have nothing and drunkenness among others. Paul's rebuke names class-based humiliation.
The pinned Greek says ‘my body, which is for you’; it does not contain ‘broken for you.’

‘Unworthy’ modifies the manner of eating and drinking. The passage links failure to discern the body with communal judgment and discipline, not with a requirement that participants be morally flawless.
vocabulary: Head, used literally and as a relational metaphor.

notes: The Greek says ‘spiritual things/people’; ‘gifts’ fits the following discussion but does not exhaust the term.
Each manifestation is given for the common good, and the one Spirit distributes gifts according to the Spirit's own will.
The body includes Jews and Greeks, enslaved and free. The translation retains the real social status of enslaved people rather than reducing it to employment.
Members perceived as weaker or less honorable receive necessity, modesty, and greater honor; the body's unity requires shared suffering and joy.
The command may be plural to the church: seek the gifts that most build others, as chapter 14 explains.
Spectacular speech, knowledge, faith, generosity, and bodily surrender are nothing without love.
The pinned Greek reads ‘so that I may boast’; a well-known variant reads ‘so that I may be burned.’
‘Does not keep an account of wrong’ uses a bookkeeping verb and does not require pretending harm never happened.
‘Bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things’ describes love's orientation; it is not a command to conceal abuse or ignore truth and justice.
‘Completeness’ is not identified more precisely in the verse; the main text avoids defining it as one later event or artifact.
vocabulary: Love expressed in committed regard and action.
Count, reckon, or keep an account.
Mirror, in antiquity typically polished metal.

notes: Uninterpreted tongues address God but do not build listeners who cannot understand. Paul values both spirit and mind and prefers five intelligible words in church to ten thousand unintelligible ones.
Paul's sign statement and the visitor scenarios create a difficult sequence. The translation preserves the tension rather than forcing one simple rule.
Tongues and prophecy are limited, interpreted, weighed, and ordered; spiritual speech is not presented as uncontrollable.

These verses command women to be silent and ask husbands at home, while 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy. Their textual placement and application are disputed; the pinned main text includes them here.
The pinned Greek reads the passive ‘is not recognized’; some witnesses read the imperative ‘let that person remain ignorant.’
vocabulary: A foreign-language speaker, heard as unintelligible.

notes: Paul recites received testimony: death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances. His image for himself in verse 8 is literally an untimely or traumatic birth.
Both clauses use ‘all.’ Verse 23 immediately gives an order beginning with Christ and then those who belong to him at his coming; the translation does not settle later debates about scope.
Baptism ‘for the dead’ is mentioned as an existing practice in an argument for resurrection. Its procedure and Paul's evaluation are not explained.
Fighting wild beasts in Ephesus may be literal or metaphorical. The main text retains the image.
‘Spiritual body’ remains a body animated and transformed by the Spirit, not a nonphysical ghost.
The pinned text says ‘we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed.’ Variant traditions arrange the negatives differently.
The pinned text repeats ‘death’ in both questions; some traditions address Hades in the second.
vocabulary: Raise up; in the perfect tense here, has been raised.
Firstfruits, the first portion anticipating the harvest.
Spiritual, characterized or animated by the Spirit.

notes: The collection is for the saints in Jerusalem, gathered locally in advance and carried by representatives approved by the Corinthians.
The open door and many opponents coexist; opportunity is not equated with lack of resistance.
Paul strongly urged Apollos to visit, but Apollos did not wish to come then. His agency is not hidden.
The Greek idiom is literally ‘act like men’; ‘be courageous’ carries its exhortational force without making courage male-only.
The whole household of Stephanas devoted themselves to service, and the church is told to submit to such laboring people.
Marana tha is Aramaic, commonly understood as ‘Our Lord, come!’ or ‘Our Lord has come.’ The form is retained because the word division is anciently ambiguous.
vocabulary: Door, here an opportunity for effective work.
